title: Nagel keeps another rate rise open as energy costs feed through
summary: Joachim Nagel thought euro area inflation would most likely ease gradually towards 2% when looking into 2027 and beyond. He also thought the ECB might have to raise rates again. The two views fit together because his forecast depends on an appropriate policy response: a decline in inflation over time is compatible with an additional increase in borrowing costs along the way. The 18 November interview gives the Bundesbank president’s assessment of the risks. It records two earlier Governing Council increases and leaves the next decision open.

The deterioration since the beginning of the year originated in energy. Nagel attributed the sharp price increase to the war involving Iran and said that the effects were still being felt. He described inflation heading into the new year as around 3% in Germany and 4% for the euro area. The distinction matters for reading his comments about wages. The collective bargaining dispute the interviewer raised concerned Germany, whereas the ECB’s target applies to the wider currency area. Nagel regarded the energy shock as appreciably less severe than the gas-price shock that followed the attack on Ukraine (opening exchange).

Near-term price pressure and the medium-term inflation path need different evidence. The interviewer cited producer prices and companies’ price expectations as reasons prices might rise further. Nagel accepted that possibility without putting a number on it. His answer turned to the prospects for a gradual decline in inflation from 2027 onwards. He expressed confidence in an eventual return to target and a desire to get there quickly, but gave neither a date for reaching 2% nor a timetable for another hike. His response to the producer-price question leaves room for additional pass-through before the annual inflation rate falls.

Wages were a reason for vigilance, although Nagel saw no evidence of a wage-price spiral at the time of the interview. The interviewer pointed to IG Metall invoking inflation in wage negotiations. Nagel judged that the lower level of German inflation relative to four years earlier reduced the danger of large second-round effects. The union’s bargaining position illustrates how households and employers can react to the initial shock. It supplies no information here about the eventual settlement, wage agreements elsewhere or how much firms would pass through to customers.

The lever Nagel identified was the cost of credit. The ECB cannot reverse the original geopolitical increase in petrol prices through its policy rate. More expensive loans can nevertheless curb spending and discourage an initial price increase from becoming entrenched. He also wanted people to remain confident that the central bank would deliver its target. His closing example illustrated the part demand can play even without a fresh policy decision: he suggested that shoppers’ resistance after earlier price increases had contributed to lower prices for a seasonal chocolate product. He offered it as an example of the limits of firms’ pricing power in one market. It supplies little basis for assessing pricing power across the economy. For a rates reader, the unresolved issue is how broad renewed price pressure becomes while the two existing increases work through credit.

questions.question: How far is the energy shock spreading into other prices?
questions.detail: Nagel allows for further near-term increases while expecting inflation to ease over a longer horizon. A rise concentrated in energy would have different implications for the persistence of tight policy from a broadening of price increases across services and manufactured goods. Compare detailed official price releases and business surveys around the interview date, separating the share of items affected from the size of the energy contribution.

questions.question: Are wage settlements absorbing the price shock or extending it?
questions.detail: The interview establishes that one union invoked inflation and that Nagel judged a wage-price spiral unlikely. It does not establish the wage increase ultimately agreed, its duration or productivity growth in the affected sector. For the likelihood of another rate rise, examine negotiated pay schedules alongside sectoral output per worker and firms’ stated pricing intentions, distinguishing one-off compensation from increases in basic pay.

questions.question: How much restraint were the two earlier increases already delivering?
questions.detail: Nagel identifies more expensive loans as the transmission channel but gives no evidence on loan pricing, volumes or borrowers’ refinancing dates. Those observations would help a rates investor judge whether another increase would add much restraint over the relevant horizon. Start with official new-loan and outstanding-loan rate statistics, credit volumes and bank lending surveys, allowing for firms reducing their demand for credit as well as banks tightening supply.
